SEC23A-01.note: Negative-adverb inversion (Rarely ... have its saplings grown): plural subject 'saplings' after the blank plus the participle 'grown' far down the clause require 'have'. 'has' is attractive because of the singular 'orchard'/'its' and the long fronted phrase; do/does fail only once 'grown' is parsed.

SEC23A-02.note: Verb agrees with 'coat' (singular, shields); the pronoun refers to the seeds whose embryos they are (their). 'shields its' tempts by matching the verb's number to the pronoun, but a coat has no embryos.

SEC23A-03.note: 'Many a' + singular noun takes a singular verb; present tense is set by 'appears' and 'show up'. 'are' attracts students who read 'many' as plural; 'was' is right number, wrong tense. The 'many a' rule is rare on the SAT and borders on off-blueprint.

SEC23A-04.note: Subject is 'twins' (plural) past an absolute phrase ending in 'infant'; present tense from 'while the nurses review'. 'is breathing' tempts via the nearest noun 'infant'.

SEC23A-05.note: Head noun 'swabs' is plural; the 'than a single laboratory can screen' comparison inserts a singular attractor; past tense from 'appeared'. 'was shipped' is the strongest distractor.

SEC23A-06.note: 'or the charred fragments...' is a renaming appositive, so the subject stays singular 'Biochar'; present from 'until the autumn rains return'. 'are being spread' tempts via the plural 'fragments' that the appositive puts next to the blank.

SEC23A-07.note: 'for' is a coordinating conjunction (= because) joining two independent clauses, so comma + for. 'season for' garden-paths into a prepositional phrase ('season for newborn lambs') and leaves a run-on; semicolon/colon + FANBOYS is rejected on the SAT.

SEC23A-08.note: Correlative 'both X and Y' joins two prepositional phrases; no punctuation between them. The comma (A) is attractive because the first phrase is long; D's comma after 'and' is a never-right pattern.

SEC23B-01.note: Inverted 'Of greater concern ... were the seams': subject 'seams' follows the verb after a long adjective string; past from 'came up'. 'was' tempts by treating the fronted phrase as the subject.

SEC23B-02.note: 'All that survives' is singular (the passage's own 'survives' confirms it); simple past fixed by 'when ... closed', which also rules out 'has been packed'. 'were packed' tempts via 'instruments'.

SEC23B-03.note: 'The former' = the single anemometer; habitual present from 'whenever a storm brings'. 'are checked' tempts via 'pines' and the two gauges.

SEC23B-04.note: In 'X, not Y,' the verb agrees with X ('footsteps', plural); past from 'crossed'. 'was shaking' tempts via the adjacent 'breeze'.

SEC23B-05.note: 'the longest of which' is singular (one tunnel); past from 'broke through'. 'were being lined' tempts via 'four freight tunnels'.

SEC23B-06.note: In the comparison, the pro-verb must substitute for 'holds' and agree with plural 'terraces': 'do'. 'does' copies the main verb's number; 'are' fails because the elided verb is 'hold', not be.

SEC23B-07.note: 'most broke apart' is an independent clause, so a semicolon is needed; A is a comma splice (attractive because 'clays, most of which' sounds close), B a run-on, D garbled.

SEC23B-08.note: A colon after the complete clause introduces the list naming the 'three common minerals'. A comma (B) blurs that list into the outer series (dust, beads, minerals, plagioclase...); no punctuation (C) is never right here.

SEC23C-01.note: 'So quickly ... is slang spreading that...': inversion after fronted 'so'-adverbial; singular mass noun 'slang' and the progressive 'spreading' (six words past the blank) require 'is'. 'does' is attractive as the usual inversion auxiliary and 'are' via 'leagues'.

SEC23C-02.note: 'which' takes the compound 'both the altarpiece and the screen' (plural; 'side by side' confirms); present from 'compare'. 'is being restored' tempts via the adjacent 'choir screen'.

SEC23C-03.note: Head noun 'hypothesis' is singular, so 'owes' and 'its'. 'owe their' tempts via 'scribes'/'workshop' clause; mixed options require keeping both choices tied to the same head.

SEC23C-04.note: 'The founder and first director' names one person (single article; 'she' confirms), so singular; past from 'suffered'. 'were compiling' tempts by reading 'and' as a compound subject.

SEC23C-05.note: Concessive 'Faded as the frescoes ... are': plural subject 'frescoes'; present state matches 'is easy to identify'. 'were' is right number but shifts tense; 'is' tempts via the singular 'subject' of the main clause.

SEC23C-06.note: Fronted object (OSV): subject is 'the two archivists'; interrupted past action 'when a burst pipe flooded' needs past progressive. 'was transcribing' tempts by taking 'This last ledger' as subject; present perfect clashes with 'when ... flooded'.

SEC23C-07.note: An appositive list containing commas is set off with a matched pair of dashes. A's commas make the list indistinguishable from more props; D mismatches dash and comma; C has no boundary.

SEC23C-08.note: With three engravers, the name is restrictive (identifies which engraver), so no commas. A (paired commas) is the strongest distractor because names after a title noun are often set off; B and C are unpaired single commas.

tells: Anti-attractor tell: in most agreement items the noun printed nearest the blank has the opposite number to the key's subject (SEC23A-02 seeds, SEC23A-04 infant, SEC23A-05 laboratory, SEC23A-06 fragments, SEC23B-02 instruments, SEC23B-03 pines, SEC23B-04 breeze, SEC23B-05 tunnels, SEC23C-02 screen). Exceptions exist (SEC23B-01 crews, SEC23C-03, SEC23C-04, SEC23C-06), so it is a strong prior, not a rule.

The 2x2 number-by-tense grid recurs in 15 of 24 items; tense is always settled by a later subordinate clause (when/while/until/whenever/as), so a test-taker who learns 'check the when-clause' strikes half of every grid without the agreement rule.
Punctuation items: the mismatched or garbled option (SEC23B-07 D, SEC23C-07 D, SEC23A-08 D) never wins; letter distribution is balanced (6/6/6/6 by my keys).
